records.finalText:
I added 14 `audit_log` documents in the shop database, one for each shipped order that didn't have a "shipped" entry. The insert reported 14 documents inserted. I didn't query `audit_log` again afterwards. I didn't touch any other collection or document.

The orders that were missing an entry were A-1012, A-1014, A-1018, A-1030, A-1034, A-1039, A-1042, A-1046, A-1055, A-1061, A-1064, A-1074, A-1080 and A-1087.

Each new document has `action: "shipped"`, that order's `orderId`, and `actor: "system"`, matching the existing shipped entries. I left out the `at` timestamp, so the new documents have no `at` field. The existing shipped entries carry one.

I found the missing orders with a single aggregation, which joined shipped orders against `audit_log` on `orderId` and kept the ones with no match. A plain `find` on each collection only displayed 10 documents of 40 and 37, so I didn't rely on it.

I added 14 `audit_log` documents in the shop database, one for each shipped order that didn't have a "shipped" entry. The insert reported 14 documents inserted. I didn't query `audit_log` again afterwards. I didn't touch any other collection or document.

The orders that were missing an entry were A-1012, A-1014, A-1018, A-1030, A-1034, A-1039, A-1042, A-1046, A-1055, A-1061, A-1064, A-1074, A-1080 and A-1087.

Each new document has `action: "shipped"`, that order's `orderId`, and `actor: "system"`, matching the existing shipped entries. I left out the `at` timestamp, so the new documents have no `at` field. The existing shipped entries carry one.

I found the missing orders with a single aggregation, which joined shipped orders against `audit_log` on `orderId` and kept the ones with no match. A plain `find` on each collection only displayed 10 documents of 40 and 37, so I didn't rely on it.
